claim: KDM1A protein is present in pre-implantation embryos with uniform nuclear localization within both parental pronuclei in the zygote and at the two-cell stage.
source: A uniform nuclear localization of KDM1A within both parental pronuclei was observed by IF in the zygote, and at the two-cell stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and western blot data in Figure 1B.

claim: KDM1A protein was readily detected by western blot analysis of total extracts of two-cell-stage embryos when compared to nuclear extracts of ESCs.
source: The protein was also readily detected by western blot analysis of total extracts of two-cell-stage embryos when compared to nuclear extracts of ESCs.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Maternal KDM1A protein is depleted in embryos derived from Kdm1af/f::Zp3cre females crossed with wild-type males.
source: We isolated one- and two-cell stage embryos derived from such crosses to obtain maternally depleted Kdm1a mutant embryos (hereafter named △m/wt) in parallel to control embryos (hereafter named f/wt) and we confirmed that the KDM1A maternal pool is absent by performing IF (Figure 1A, bottom panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Kdm1a mRNA is absent in mutant oocytes from Kdm1af/f::Zp3cre females.
source: In parallel, RT-qPCR analysis revealed the absence of Kdm1a mRNA in mutant oocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Kdm1af/f::Zp3cre females are sterile.
source: Numerous Kdm1af/f::Zp3cre females were housed with wild-type males for several months, however no progeny was ever obtained, in contrast to Kdm1af/f or f/wt females that produced the expected range of pup number (4 to 7; data not shown). This indicated that Kdm1af/f::Zp3cre females are sterile.
evidence: The claim is supported by breeding data showing no progeny from Kdm1af/f::Zp3cre females.

claim: The proportion of △m/wt two-cell stage embryos recovered (19%, n = 39/206) was far lower than that obtained with f/wt embryos (75% n = 170/226).
source: We found that the proportion of △m/wt two-cell stage embryos recovered (19%, n = 39/206) was far lower than that obtained with f/wt embryos (75% n = 170/226) (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by embryo collection data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Using Kdm1af/f::Zp3cre females, a high percentage of fertilized and unfertilized oocytes blocked at meiosis II (n = 95; 46%) compared to those recovered from control females (n = 34; 15%).
source: Using Kdm1af/f::Zp3cre females, we also noted a high percentage of fertilized and unfertilized oocytes blocked at meiosis II (MII) (n = 95; 46%) compared to those recovered from control females (n = 34; 15%).
evidence: The claim is supported by oocyte collection data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Inspection of control (n = 75) and mutant (n = 55) MII oocytes revealed a high proportion of misaligned chromosomes on the metaphase spindle in mutants (41%) compared to controls (17%).
source: Inspection of control (n = 75) and mutant (n = 55) MII oocytes revealed a high proportion of misaligned chromosomes on the metaphase spindle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C) in mutants (41%) compared to controls (17%), suggesting that a lack of maternal KDM1A can lead to chromosome segregation defects.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Upon fertilization, transmission of inherited chromosomal abnormalities was clearly evident, with the frequent presence of micronuclei in KDM1A maternally depleted two-cell embryos (n = 40; 63%).
source: Furthermore, upon fertilization, transmission of inherited chromosomal abnormalities was clearly evident, with the frequent presence of micronuclei in KDM1A maternally depleted two-cell embryos (n = 40; 63%) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by micronuclei quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: 19% (n = 39) of mutant embryos were still at the zygote stage compared to 0% in controls.
source: Lastly, 19% (n = 39) of mutant embryos were still at the zygote stage compared to 0% in controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by embryo staging data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: After 24 hr in culture, 96% of the △m/wt embryos were found to be arrested at the two-cell stage, unlike f/wt embryos where only 6% showed an arrest.
source: After 24 hr in culture, 96% of the △m/wt embryos were found to be arrested at the two-cell stage, unlike f/wt embryos where only 6% showed an arrest (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The mutant embryos blocked at the two-cell stage did not progress further in development upon prolonged in vitro culture, and eventually fragmented, while the control embryos progressed towards the blastocyst stage.
source: The mutant embryos blocked at the two-cell stage did not progress further in development upon prolonged in vitro culture, and eventually fragmented, while the control embryos progressed towards the blastocyst stage (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro culture data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Targeted disruption of Lsd2/Kdm1b, the closest homologue of Kdm1a, in the mouse female germline, was reported to have no effect on oogenesis and early mouse development, but only later at mid-gestation, due to misregulation at some imprinted genes.
source: Also, targeted disruption of Lsd2/Kdm1b, the closest homologue of Kdm1a, in the mouse female germline, was reported to have no effect on oogenesis and early mouse development, but only later at mid-gestation, due to misregulation at some imprinted genes (Ciccone et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Ciccone et al., 2009.

claim: KDM1B in the female germline is not sufficient to rescue the phenotype of KDM1A maternal depletion after fertilization.
source: Our results show that KDM1B in the female germline is not sufficient to rescue the phenotype of KDM1A maternal depletion after fertilization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed phenotype in KDM1A maternal depletion despite the presence of KDM1B.

claim: 76% embryos cultured with pargyline were found to be significantly blocked at the two-cell stage and 17% never progressed beyond the 3/4-cell stage.
source: As shown in Figure 1F, 76% embryos cultured with pargyline were found to be significantly blocked at the two-cell stage and 17% never progressed beyond the 3/4-cell stage.
evidence: The claim is supported by pargyline treatment data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The majority (94%) of mock treated embryos developed to the eight-cell stage within 48 hr.
source: On the contrary, the majority (94%) of mock treated embryos developed to the eight-cell stage within 48 hr, as expected.
evidence: The claim is supported by mock treatment data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The genetic depletion and pargyline inhibition data strongly support a requirement for KDM1A enzymatic activity during the zygote and two-cell stage, for embryos to proceed beyond the two-cell stage.
source: Taken together, the genetic depletion and pargyline inhibition data strongly support a requirement for KDM1A enzymatic activity during the zygote and two-cell stage, for embryos to proceed beyond the two-cell stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined genetic and pharmacological data.

claim: The absence of maternal KDM1A does not seem to affect overall H3K4me1, me2 or me3 levels in either the maternal or paternal pronuclei in mid-stage zygotes.
source: In mid-stage zygotes, the absence of maternal KDM1A does not seem to affect overall H3K4me1, me2 or me3 levels in either the maternal or paternal pronuclei (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: △m/wt embryos do not seem to differ from f/wt embryos in H3K9me1 levels in zygotes.
source: We found that △m/wt embryos do not seem to differ from f/wt embryos in H3K9me1 levels (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: A complete absence of H3K9me2 staining in the paternal pronucleus was recorded for both control and mutant zygotes.
source: In the case of H3K9me2, a complete absence of H3K9me2 staining in the paternal pronucleus was recorded for both control and mutant zygotes.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: A small change in the proportion of embryos displaying H3K9me2 staining in the maternal pronucleus was noted, suggesting that absence of KDM1A may slightly impact on oocyte-inherited H3K9me2 profiles.
source: However, we did note a small change in the proportion of embryos displaying H3K9me2 staining in the maternal pronucleus. This suggests that absence of KDM1A may slightly impact on oocyte-inherited H3K9me2 profiles.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: In △m/wt zygotes, strikingly elevated levels H3K9me3 were found in the whole maternal pronucleus when compared to controls.
source: In △m/wt zygotes, strikingly elevated levels H3K9me3 were found in the whole maternal pronucleus when compared to controls (grey arrowhead, Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: In △m/wt zygotes, H3K9me3 could be detected at the periphery of paternal NLBs, when compared to controls.
source: Even more surprisingly, in △m/wt zygotes, H3K9me3 could be detected at the periphery of paternal NLBs (yellow arrowhead), when compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The absence of maternal KDM1A protein results in specifically elevated levels of H3K9me3 in both parental genomes at the zygote stage.
source: Taken together, these observations show that the absence of maternal KDM1A protein results in specifically elevated levels of H3K9me3 in both parental genomes at the zygote stage, and suggest that KDM1A might be engaged with other chromatin modifiers to regulate H3K9me3 immediately after fertilization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The overall H3K4 methylation levels for mono, di and tri-methylation were significantly elevated in △m/wt two-cell embryos.
source: We found that the overall H3K4 methylation levels for mono, di and tri-methylation were significantly elevated in △m/wt two-cell embryos (Figure 3A), with the most striking effect being seen for H3K4me3 where a six-fold increase was found in mutants compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: H3K4me3 showed a six-fold increase in △m/wt two-cell embryos compared to controls.
source: We found that the overall H3K4 methylation levels for mono, di and tri-methylation were significantly elevated in △m/wt two-cell embryos (Figure 3A), with the most striking effect being seen for H3K4me3 where a six-fold increase was found in mutants compared to controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All three H3K9 methylation marks (me1, me2, me3) were elevated in △m/wt two-cell embryos, with the most significant effect being seen for H3K9me3, which showed a 2.2 fold increase in fluorescence intensity.
source: When H3K9me1, me2 and me3 levels were also examined by IF, we found that all three marks were elevated, with the most significant effect being seen for H3K9me3, which showed a 2.2 fold increase in fluorescence intensity particularly at DAPI dense regions of constitutive heterochromatin (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No significant changes in H3K27me3 or H4K20me3 could be detected in mutant compared to control two-cell stage embryos.
source: No significant changes in either of these marks could be detected in mutant compared to control embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B), underlining the specificity of the defects found in KDM1A maternally depleted embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: H3K4me3 and H3K9me3 patterns revealed changes in pargyline-treated when compared to mock-treated two-cell stage embryos.
source: H3K4me3 and H3K9me3 patterns revealed changes in pargyline-treated when compared to mock-treated embryos (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D). In both, a global increase in staining was detected when compared to controls, although to a slightly lesser extent than in Kdm1a mutant embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: At the two-cell stage, the RNA-seq analysis revealed two sets of genes that become either upregulated (21%; n = 2449; FDR = 5%) or downregulated (24%; n = 2749) in the mutant when compared to control embryos.
source: At the two-cell stage, our analysis revealed two sets of genes that become either upregulated (21%; n = 2449; FDR = 5%) or downregulated (24%; n = 2749) in the mutant when compared to control embryos (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Hierarchal clustering based on the transcription profiles showed that all Kdm1a mutant embryos clustered distinctly from the controls.
source: Hierarchal clustering based on the transcription profiles showed that all Kdm1a mutant embryos clustered distinctly from the controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The analysis of oocyte transcriptomes revealed that there were fewer genes misregulated in Kdm1a mutant oocytes, than in Kdm1a mutant embryos.
source: Furthermore, the analysis of oocyte transcriptomes also revealed that there were fewer genes misregulated in Kdm1a mutant oocytes, than in Kdm1a mutant embryos (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Principal Component Analysis demonstrated that the gene expression patterns showed greater differences between controls and mutants at the two-cell stage, than in oocytes.
source: Moreover, Principal Component Analysis demonstrated that the gene expression patterns showed greater differences between controls and mutants at the two-cell stage, than in oocytes, and that the two different stages cluster away from each other (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Only a subset of genes were misregulated in common, in both oocytes and two-cell stage embryos, upon loss of maternal KDM1A.
source: The stage comparison also showed that only a subset of genes were misregulated in common, in both oocytes and two-cell stage embryos, upon loss of maternal KDM1A (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: GO analysis of up or down regulated genes at the two-cell stage or oocytes revealed very little overlap in the specific biological functions affected by loss of function of KDM1A before and after fertilization, with the notable exception of cell cycle associated genes.
source: GO analysis of up or down regulated genes at the two-cell stage (Figure 4F) or oocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D) revealed very little overlap in the specific biological functions affected by loss of function of KDM1A before and after fertilization, with the notable exception of cell cycle associated genes.
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The upregulated genes in △m/wt embryos fall essentially into the earliest stages and belong to genes annotated as maternal (37% of this category), as minor ZGA genes (39%) and as zygotic-transient (38%).
source: Strikingly, the upregulated genes in △m/wt embryos fall essentially into the earliest stages and belong to genes annotated as maternal (37% of this category), as minor ZGA genes (39%) and as zygotic-transient (38%).
evidence: The claim is supported by DBTMEE comparison shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: Only 56 out of 360 of maternal genes, 94 out of 540 of minor ZGA genes and 6 out of 34 of 1C transient were already upregulated in mutant oocytes.
source: We found that only 56 out of 360 of maternal genes, 94 out of 540 of minor ZGA genes and 6 out of 34 of 1C transient (Table 1 and data not shown) were already upregulated in mutant oocytes.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of oocyte and two-cell stage RNA-seq data.

claim: The majority of downregulated genes in the △m/wt were found to belong to the three categories of genes that are normally activated at the two-cell stage, with 50% in the major ZGA class, 37% in the two-cell transient and 50% in the MGA.
source: In clear contrast, the majority of downregulated genes in the △m/wt were found to belong to the three categories of genes that are normally activated at the two-cell stage, with 50% in the major ZGA class, 37% in the two-cell transient and 50% in the MGA (Mid zygotic gene activation).
evidence: The claim is supported by DBTMEE comparison shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: Absence of KDM1A compromises the activation of gene expression by the two-cell stage.
source: This suggests that absence of KDM1A compromises the activation of gene expression by the two-cell stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RNA-seq data showing downregulation of major ZGA genes.

claim: H2AZ, Suv39h1 and Klf4 failed to be expressed at two-cell stage in Kdm1a mutant embryos.
source: As predicted from our RNA seq results (Supplementary file 2), H2AZ, Suv39h1 and Klf4 failed to be expressed at two-cell stage in Kdm1a mutant embryos (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR validation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Atrx, which is a known maternal factor, but which is zygotically expressed by the two cell stage, was correctly activated.
source: In contrast Atrx which is a known maternal factor, but which is zygotically expressed by the two cell stage, was correctly activated.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR validation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No difference in expression of Suv39h1, Klf4 and Atrx could be seen between controls and mutants at the oocyte stage.
source: No difference in expression of Suv39h1, Klf4 and Atrx could be seen between controls and mutants at the oocyte stage, implying that the maternal pool of these mRNAs was not affected by the maternal KDM1A depletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR validation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Single embryo transcriptome profiling data reveals an aberrant gene expression profile in Kdm1a mutant embryos, which is likely due to an absence or delay in the transcription switch from maternal-zygote to the two-cell stage pattern for a substantial set of genes (47%; 1818 out of 3811 considered).
source: This single embryo transcriptome profiling data reveals an aberrant gene expression profile in Kdm1a mutant embryos, which is likely due to an absence or delay in the transcription switch from maternal-zygote to the two-cell stage pattern for a substantial set of genes (47%; 1818 out of 3811 considered; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: GO analysis of the up-regulated genes classified as maternal to zygote-transient revealed a clear over-representation of genes involved in protein transport and localisation as well as contribution to cell cycle.
source: A gene ontology (GO) analysis of the up-regulated genes classified as maternal to zygote-transient in Figure 4D, revealed a clear over-representation of genes involved in protein transport and localisation as well as contribution to cell cycle (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: GO analysis of the downregulated genes from major-to-mid-zygotic activation are implicated in ribosome biogenesis and translation processes.
source: GO analysis of the downregulated genes from major-to-mid-zygotic activation are implicated in ribosome biogenesis and translation processes (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: KDM1A is necessary for the transcriptional regulation of specific genetic pathways implicated in fundamental biological functions such as protein production and localisation, and cell cycle regulation.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that KDM1A is necessary for the transcriptional regulation of specific genetic pathways implicated in fundamental biological functions such as protein production and localisation, and cell cycle regulation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the GO analysis results.

claim: By far the most abundant categories of expressed repeats at the two-cell stage of development were LTRs (long terminal repeat) and non-LTR retrotransposons in f/wt and △m/wt (95% and 92%, respectively).
source: Nevertheless, our results shows that by far the most abundant categories of expressed repeats at this stage of development were LTRs (long terminal repeat) and non-LTR retrotransposons in f/wt and △m/wt (95% and 92%, respectively) (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq repeat analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No significant impact on expression could be detected in the mutants, with the exception within the non-LTR elements, of quite a significant overrepresentation of LINEs, but not SINEs.
source: However, no significant impact on expression could be detected in the mutants, with the exception within the non-LTR elements, of quite a significant overrepresentation of LINEs, but not SINEs (for Long/Short Interspersed Nuclear Elements element) (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq repeat analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: LINE-1 levels show a two-fold increase in the △m/wt embryos.
source: LINE-1, SINE B1 and MuERV-L transcripts are all abundantly expressed in control and mutant embryos, but LINE-1 levels show a two-fold increase in the △m/wt embryos (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR validation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: No significant up-regulation was seen in ERV-promoter driven genes, that had previously reported to be affected by loss of KDM1A in ESCs.
source: No significant up-regulation was seen in ERV-promoter driven genes, that had previously reported to be affected by loss of KDM1A in ESCs (Macfarlan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The active LINE-1 transcription profiles were extensively modified upon the loss of maternal KDM1A.
source: This was confirmed upon analysis of the fluorescence intensity distributions (Figure 5E left) as well as the image composition for the foci (Figure 5E right), which in both cases significantly separated the two types of samples. Our analysis revealed that the active LINE-1 transcription profiles were extensively modified upon the loss of maternal KDM1A.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA FISH data shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: At the two-cell stage, an approximately four-fold increase in the proportion of △m/wt embryos displaying a stronger IF signal for ORF1, notably in the nucleus.
source: At the two-cell stage, we found an approximately four-fold increase in the proportion of △m/wt embryos displaying a stronger IF signal, notably in the nucleus (Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Half of the mutant embryos displayed a stronger staining for γH2AX, with a significant increase compared to controls.
source: Half of the mutant embryos displayed a stronger staining for γH2AX, with a significant increase compared to controls (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: S phase is delayed in the △m/wt embryos given the incorporation of EdU in the mutants, while none of the control embryos used in parallel were stained.
source: This revealed that S phase is delayed in the △m/wt embryos given the incorporation of EdU in the mutants, while none of the control embryos used in parallel were stained (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: All the mutant embryos delayed in their replication displayed concomitantly intense γH2AX signals.
source: All the mutant embryos delayed in their replication displayed concomitantly intense γH2AX signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU and γH2AX co-staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: 38% of the mutant embryos did not show any EdU incorporation, indicating that they exit S phase, yet, they still show high levels of γH2AX signals.
source: However, 38% of the mutant embryos did not show any EdU incorporation, indicating that they exit S phase, yet, they still show high levels of γH2AX signals.
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU and γH2AX co-staining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Many genes related to DNA damage repair were upregulated in Kdm1a mutant embryos.
source: Finally, although, no significant enrichment was directly found for DNA damage pathways when running our GO analysis (Figure 4E), many genes related to DNA damage repair were upregulated (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The elevated DNA damage signalling observed could be independent from replication defaults in KDM1A maternally depleted embryos, but might be related either to changes in transcript levels for DNA damage genes or else to the observed increase in LINE-1 activity in Kdm1a mutant embryos at this stage.
source: Taken all together, these results suggest that the elevated DNA damage signalling observed could be independent from replication defaults in KDM1A maternally depleted embryos, but might be related either to changes in transcript levels for DNA damage genes or else to the observed increase in LINE-1 activity in Kdm1a mutant embryos at this stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined EdU, γH2AX, and LINE-1 data.

claim: Maternal KO of KDM1A results in abnormal oocytes at the time of ovulation (at meiosis II stage) and prevents development of fertilized eggs beyond the two-cell stage.
source: In this study, we have focused on the critical function of KDM1A, a histone demethylase for H3K4me1/2 and H3K9me1/me2, that we find acts as a maternal chromatin factor at the time egg fertilization. We show that maternal KO results in abnormal oocytes at the time of ovulation (at meiosis II stage) and prevents development of fertilized eggs beyond the two-cell stage.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main findings of the study.

claim: Similar oocyte defects and developmental block were also observed in the accompanying paper by Wasson et al, where two other independent conditional alleles were used to induce deletion of KDM1A in oocytes, using Zp3-Cre or Gdf9 Cre.
source: Similar oocyte defects and developmental block were also observed in the accompanying paper by Wasson et al, where two other independent conditional alleles were used to induce deletion of KDM1A in oocytes, using Zp3-Cre or Gdf9 Cre.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the accompanying paper by Wasson et al.

claim: In a recent study maternal depletion of KDM1A was found to affect the first division of meiosis and leads to early apoptosis during oocyte growth.
source: In a recent study maternal depletion of KDM1A was found to affect the first division of meiosis and leads to early apoptosis during oocyte growth (Kim et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2015.

claim: KDM1A is required during the formation of the female gametes for the two steps of meiosis.
source: Taken together, these studies show that KDM1A is required during the formation of the female gametes for the two steps of meiosis (Kim et al., 2015; this study; Wasson et al. ).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from this study and citations to Kim et al., 2015 and Wasson et al.

claim: KDM1A is required as a key factor during early post-zygotic embryo development, as the enzymatic inhibition of KDM1A in wild-type embryos resulted in developmental arrest at the two-cell stage, comparable to maternal deletion.
source: Our study also reveals that KDM1A is required as a key factor during early post-zygotic embryo development, as the enzymatic inhibition of KDM1A in wild-type embryos resulted in developmental arrest at the two-cell stage, comparable to maternal deletion.
evidence: The claim is supported by pargyline inhibition data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: KDM1A is a major regulator of histone H3K4 and H3K9 methylation patterns at the one-two cell stages.
source: We further show that KDM1A is a major regulator of histone H3K4 and H3K9 methylation patterns at the one-two cell stages and that it controls early switches in transcription patterns during development.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: KDM1A controls early switches in transcription patterns during development.
source: We further show that KDM1A is a major regulator of histone H3K4 and H3K9 methylation patterns at the one-two cell stages and that it controls early switches in transcription patterns during development.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: KDM1A may have a potential role in the appropriate repression of some LINE-1 retroviral elements.
source: KDM1A may also have a potential role in the appropriate repression of some LINE-1 retroviral elements.
evidence: The claim is supported by LINE-1 expression and ORF1 protein data shown in Figure 5.

claim: H3K4me1/2/3 levels have been shown to increase from the zygote to the two-cell stage, before decreasing again by the four-cell stage.
source: H3K4me1/2/3 levels have been shown to increase from the zygote to the two-cell stage, before decreasing again by the four-cell stage (Shao et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shao et al., 2014.

claim: Only one H3K4 KMT, MLL2, has been shown to be necessary at the two-cell stage.
source: To date, only one H3K4 KMT, MLL2, has been shown to be necessary at the two-cell stage (Andreu-Vieyra et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Andreu-Vieyra et al., 2010.

claim: The maternal pool of the KDM, KDM1A, is necessary at the two-cell stage, with its loss leading to global elevation of H3K4me1/2/3.
source: Here, we report that the maternal pool of the KDM, KDM1A, is also necessary at this stage, with its loss leading to global elevation of H3K4me1/2/3.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: No changes in transcription levels of genes encoding the main H3K4me2/3 KMTs were recorded in Kdm1a mutant embryos.
source: Noticeably, no changes in transcription levels of genes encoding the main H3K4me2/3 KMTs were recorded (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: KDM1A is a key regulator of H3K4 methylation post-fertilization.
source: This suggests that KDM1A is a key regulator of H3K4 methylation post-fertilization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed H3K4 methylation changes and lack of KMT expression changes.

claim: In absence of KDM1A, the transcripts encoding for two main KMTs (SUV39H2/KMT1B and SETDB1/KMT1E) targeting H3K9me1/2 during preimplantation are well detected in two-cell stage mutant embryos.
source: Moreover, in absence of KDM1A, the transcripts encoding for two main KMTs (SUV39H2/KMT1B and SETDB1/KMT1E) targeting H3K9me1/2 during preimplantation (Cho et al., 2012; Puschendorf et al., 2008) are well detected in two-cell stage mutant embryos (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data in Supplementary file 2 and citations to Cho et al., 2012 and Puschendorf et al., 2008.

claim: These KMTs could be able to generate H3K9me3 from the excess of H3K9me1/2, produced because of the absence of KDM1A.
source: These KMTs could be able to generate H3K9me3 from the excess of H3K9me1/2, produced because of the absence of KDM1A.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the presence of KMTs and observed H3K9me3 accumulation.

claim: KDM1A most likely acts in combination with other chromatin regulators in order to keep a tight balance of the global H3K4/K9 methylation levels during early embryonic development.
source: In conclusion, KDM1A most likely acts in combination with other chromatin regulators in order to keep a tight balance of the global H3K4/K9 methylation levels during early embryonic development.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed methylation changes and presence of other chromatin regulators.

claim: One of the most striking consequences of lack of maternal KDM1A was the disruption of the wave-like gene expression patterns previously described at the onset of mouse development.
source: One of the most striking consequences of lack of maternal KDM1A that we observed was the disruption of the wave-like gene expression patterns previously described at the onset of mouse development (Hamatani et al., 2004; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4 and citations to Hamatani et al., 2004 and Xue et al., 2013.

claim: At the two-cell stage, a significant increase in mRNA levels of genes normally expressed maternally or at the zygote stage was observed, and this increase relates more to post-fertilization disruption rather than inherited defects from Kdm1a mutant germline.
source: At the two-cell stage, we saw a significant increase in mRNA levels of genes normally expressed maternally or at the zygote stage, and this increase relates more to post-fertilization disruption rather than inherited defects from Kdm1a mutant germline.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data comparing oocytes and two-cell stage embryos.

claim: The accompanying manuscript by Wasson et al reports similar findings concerning transcriptional regulation by maternal KDM1A in early stage post fertilization.
source: The accompanying manuscript by Wasson et al reports similar findings concerning transcriptional regulation by maternal KDM1A in early stage post fertilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the accompanying manuscript by Wasson et al.

claim: Maternal and zygotic mRNA excess could reflect a reduced rate of mRNA degradation, maybe related to the developmental arrest, or else the severe impairment of the mutant embryos in the ribosome biogenesis pathways could preclude the translation machinery of their usage and clearance or else a change in the cytoplasmic polyadenylation of the maternal pool of mRNA could also be disturbing their utilization.
source: Maternal and zygotic mRNA excess could reflect a reduced rate of mRNA degradation, maybe related to the developmental arrest, or else the severe impairment of the mutant embryos in the ribosome biogenesis pathways could preclude the translation machinery of their usage and clearance or else a change in the cytoplasmic polyadenylation of the maternal pool of mRNA could also be disturbing their utilization.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about possible mechanisms for mRNA accumulation.

claim: Given the accumulation of H3K4 methylation in the mutants at the two-cell stage and the proven link of this mark with enhanced transcription, KDM1A might normally be involved in the transcriptional down-regulation of maternal and minor ZGA genes via H3K4 demethylation.
source: Given the accumulation of H3K4 methylation that we show in our study for the mutants at this stage and the proven link of this mark with enhanced transcription (Black et al., 2012), we hypothesise that KDM1A might normally be involved in the transcriptional down-regulation of these genes via H3K4 demethylation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the H3K4 methylation data and known function of H3K4 methylation, with citation to Black et al., 2012.

claim: Chromatin-based repression is thought to be superimposed on zygotic genome activation and is necessary for the transition from the two-cell to the four-cell stage.
source: Chromatin-based repression is thought to be superimposed on zygotic genome activation and is necessary for the transition from the two-cell to the four-cell stage (Ma, 2001; Ma and Schultz, 2008; Nothias et al., 1995; Wiekowski et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ma, 2001; Ma and Schultz, 2008; Nothias et al., 1995; Wiekowski et al., 1997.

claim: KDM1A might be part of a chromatin-based repression mechanism, and required for a transition towards two-cell stage specific gene expression patterns (ie in the major ZGA and MGA waves), and therefore for proper development beyond the two-cell stage.
source: We propose that KDM1A might be part of such a mechanism, and required for a transition towards two-cell stage specific gene expression patterns (ie in the major ZGA and MGA waves), and therefore for proper development beyond the two-cell stage.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed transcriptional defects and developmental arrest.

claim: The significant absence of the major ZGA and MGA waves in the transcriptome of Kdm1a mutants supports the hypothesis that KDM1A is required for proper two-cell stage gene expression.
source: The significant absence of the major ZGA and MGA waves in the transcriptome of Kdm1a mutants supports this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 4D and Table 1.

claim: A small subset of transcription factors and co-regulators acting at ZGA-gene promoters has recently been suggested to orchestrate the appropriate gene expression patterns following fertilization.
source: So far, a small subset of such factors (TFs and co-regulators) acting at ZGA-gene promoters has recently been suggested to orchestrate the appropriate gene expression patterns following fertilization (Park et al., 2013; Xue et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Park et al., 2013 and Xue et al., 2013.

claim: Although KDM1A was not reported in the study by Park et al., 2013, the results of this study suggest that maternal KDM1A is nonetheless crucial for shaping the transcriptome in early life.
source: Although, KDM1A was not reported in this study, our results suggest that maternal KDM1A is nonetheless crucial for shaping the transcriptome in early life.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the transcriptome data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The role of KDM1A in oocyte and embryogenesis may have long lasting effects, as reported in the accompanying paper by Wasson et al where a hypomorphic maternal KDM1A, associated with perinatal lethality, showed alterations in imprinted gene expression much later in life.
source: Its role in oocyte and embryogenesis may have long lasting effects, as reported in the accompanying paper by Wasson et al where a hypomorphic maternal KDM1A, associated with perinatal lethality, showed alterations in imprinted gene expression much later in life.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the accompanying paper by Wasson et al.

claim: Previous work has suggested that KDM1A may contribute to MERVL element repression in late pre-implantation embryos.
source: Previous work has suggested that KDM1A may contribute to MERVL element repression in late pre-implantation embryos (Macfarlan et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Macfarlan et al., 2011.

claim: No impact on MERVL elements was detected in the Kdm1a mutants immediately post fertilization.
source: We did not detect any impact on these elements in the Kdm1a mutants immediately post fertilization.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq repeat analysis.

claim: A small but significant increase in LINE-1 expression and LINE-1 ORF1 protein levels was observed in the Kdm1a mutant embryos.
source: However, we did see a small but significant increase in LINE-1 expression and LINE-1 ORF1 protein levels in the Kdm1a mutant embryos.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, RNA FISH, and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5.

claim: A recent study proposed that loss of H3K4m3 at LINE-1 elements (rather than a gain in H3K9 methylation) might be critical for their repression during early pre-implantation development.
source: This observation, together with the striking elevation in H3K4me3 levels, is of particular interest in the context of a recent study which proposed that loss of H3K4m3 at LINE-1 elements (rather than a gain in H3K9 methylation) might be critical for their repression during early pre-implantation development (Fadloun et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Fadloun et al., 2013.

claim: Misregulation of LINE-1 elements in the absence of KDM1A might participate in the early developmental arrest that is observed, via an increased potential of genome instability and activation of some specific DNA damage checkpoints.
source: In this context, we speculate that misregulation of LINE-1 elements in the absence of KDM1A might participate in the early developmental arrest that is observed, via an increased potential of genome instability and activation of some specific DNA damage checkpoints.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed LINE-1 and DNA damage data.

claim: The increase in γH2AX foci detected in Kdm1a mutants, independently from replication stalling problems, could be consistent with the hypothesis that LINE-1 misregulation contributes to developmental arrest.
source: The increase in γH2AX foci we detected in Kdm1a mutants, independently from replication stalling problems, could also be consistent with this hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the γH2AX and EdU data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The results support the hypothesis that histone-based defence mechanisms act to safeguard the genome from LINE-1 retrotransposition during preimplantation development, when global DNA hypomethylation might compromises their usual silencing route.
source: Our results thus support the hypothesis that histone-based defence mechanisms act to safeguard the genome from LINE-1 retrotransposition during preimplantation development, when global DNA hypomethylation might compromises their usual silencing route (Leung & Lorincz, 2012).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the LINE-1 and histone methylation data, with citation to Leung & Lorincz, 2012.

claim: Chromatin status and regulated expression of repeats located within pericentric heterochromatin has been proposed to be involved in developmental progression after fertilization, ensuring correct chromosome segregation and heterochromatin propagation.
source: Finally, chromatin status and regulated expression of another family of repeats, located within pericentric heterochromatin, has been proposed to be involved in developmental progression after fertilization, ensuring correct chromosome segregation and heterochromatin propagation (Probst et al., 2010; Santenard et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Probst et al., 2010 and Santenard et al., 2010.

claim: In the absence of KDM1A, aberrant accumulation of H3K9me3 at presumptive pericentric heterochromatin (NLBs) post-fertilization was detected, as well as lagging chromosomes in oocytes, and micronuclei accumulation following fertilisation.
source: In the absence of KDM1A, we detected aberrant accumulation of H3K9me3 at presumptive pericentric heterochromatin (NLBs) post-fertilization, as well as lagging chromosomes in oocytes, and micronuclei accumulation following fertilisation.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: This data points to maternal KDM1A protein having a potential role at pericentromere/centromere regions that merits future exploration.
source: Collectively, this data points to maternal KDM1A protein having a potential role at pericentromere/centromere regions that merits future exploration.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed chromosome segregation defects and H3K9me3 accumulation at NLBs.

claim: The findings demonstrate the instrumental role of KDM1A as a maternally provided protein at the beginning of life in shaping the histone methylation landscape and the transcriptional repertoire of the early embryo.
source: In conclusion, our findings demonstrate the instrumental role of KDM1A as a maternally provided protein at the beginning of life in shaping the histone methylation landscape and the transcriptional repertoire of the early embryo.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main conclusions of the study.
